intro/hello: This is chapter two: the Transformer.
intro/paper: In twenty seventeen, a team at Google published a paper with a bold title: Attention Is All You Need. It described a translation model with no recurrence at all.
intro/block: Instead of reading a sentence one word at a time, every word looks at every other word at once. And the model is a single block, repeated.
intro/everywhere: That same block became BERT and GPT, then vision models, then the chat models of today.
intro/recipe: Here is the whole recipe. Turn tokens into vectors and add their positions. Run a stack of blocks. Then read off a score for every possible next word.
intro/inside: Inside each block are just two steps. Attention lets the tokens share information, and a small MLP then works on each token alone.
intro/plan: We will build the block piece by piece: queries, keys and values, the scaling, many heads, the mask, positions, and the wiring around them.
intro/why: But first: why throw recurrence away at all?
why/rnn: A recurrent network reads a sentence like a ticker tape: one token at a time, folding each one into a hidden state.
why/wait: Every step needs the result of the step before. So fifty tokens means fifty steps in a row, while the GPU, built to do thousands of things at once, mostly waits.
why/far: Information also has to travel. For the last word to use the first, it must survive every update in between, and so must the gradient, on its way back.
why/lstm: LSTMs help, but the path is still long.
why/attn: Attention changes the picture. Every token connects to every other token directly, so the first word and the last are a single step apart.
why/parallel: And there is no loop over time. A whole layer is a few matrix multiplies, with every position computed at once.
why/cost: The price: every token is compared with every token. For T tokens that is a T by T grid of scores, so doubling the length quadruples the work.
why/worth: For sentences, that price is small, and the speed-up in training was enormous.
qkv/tokens: Start with six tokens: the cat sat on the mat.
qkv/rows: Each token is a vector of numbers, its embedding. Stack them as rows, and you have a matrix, X: six rows, four columns.
qkv/roles: In self-attention, every token plays three roles at once.
qkv/query: A query: what am I looking for?
qkv/key: A key: what do I contain, for others to find?
qkv/value: And a value: what do I hand over, if someone attends to me?
qkv/qkvname: The names come from databases: a query is matched against every key, and the matching entries hand back their values. Here the match is soft.
qkv/matrices: Each role comes from its own learned matrix. Multiply X by W Q, and every row becomes that token's query.
qkv/same: W K makes the keys, and W V makes the values. Three matrix multiplies, and every token has all three.
qkv/why3: Why three different matrices? Because what a word looks for is not what it offers. A verb might look for its subject, while what it offers is: I am an action, in the past tense.
qkv/shapes: Notice the shapes. Six by four, times four by two, gives six by two. One row per token, all the way through.
scores/compare: Now the lookup. Take one token, sat, and compare its query with every key, using a dot product.
scores/grid: Do that for every token, and you get a six by six grid of scores. Row i, column j: how well token j matches what token i is looking for.
scores/onemm: And the whole grid is one matrix multiply: Q times K transposed, divided by a constant we will come back to.
scores/softmax: Each row then goes through a softmax: exponentiate, and divide by the row's total.
scores/weights: Now every row is a set of weights, all positive, adding up to one. This grid is the attention matrix, A.
scores/sat: Here, sat puts its biggest weight on cat: thirty six percent. These toy weights happen to make the verb look for its noun.
scores/mix: Last, each token's output is a blend of all the values, mixed in the proportions its row chose.
scores/mm: That is A times V: one more matrix multiply, for every token at once.
scores/same: Notice the two rows for the. They are identical at every step. Nothing so far tells the model that they sit in different places. Keep that in mind.
scores/total: So self-attention is three projections, two matrix multiplies and a softmax. No loops, and no idea how long the sentence is.
scaling/skipped: We skipped a detail: the division by the square root of d k. It decides whether the model can learn at all.
scaling/random: Picture queries and keys made of random numbers, with average zero and spread one: roughly what they look like when training starts.
scaling/sum: A dot product adds up d k products. Each product has a variance of one, and the variances of independent numbers add up.
scaling/grow: So the dot product has a variance of d k, and a typical score is about the square root of d k.
scaling/watch: Watch the scores spread out as the width grows. At sixty four, the width in the paper, a typical score is about eight.
scaling/softmax: Now feed scores that big into a softmax.
scaling/saturate: One key grabs almost all the weight, and the rest get almost nothing. The softmax has saturated.
scaling/gradient: And a saturated softmax has almost no gradient. Nudge any score, and the weights barely move, so the queries and keys get no signal to learn from.
scaling/fix: The fix is a single division. Divide every score by the square root of d k, and the spread goes back to one, whatever the width.
scaling/soft: The softmax is soft again, and the gradient can flow.
heads/budget: One row of weights per token is a tight budget. Sat might want to know who sat, and where, at the same time.
heads/many: So run several attentions side by side. Each one is called a head, and each has its own small W Q, W K and W V.
heads/prev: Here are four heads, built by hand. The first looks at the previous word.
heads/next: The second looks at the next word.
heads/nouns: The third finds the nouns: cat and mat.
heads/sameword: And the fourth links a word to its other copies, like the two thes.
heads/how: None of this is magic. Each pattern is just a choice of two matrices, W Q and W K. The position heads read position features, and the word heads read the words.
heads/concat: Each head returns a narrow result. Lay them side by side, and you are back to the full width.
heads/wo: One more matrix, W O, mixes what the heads found into one vector per token.
heads/cost: Eight heads of width sixty four cost about as much as one head of width five hundred and twelve. What you gain is eight separate places to look.
mask/lm: A language model learns to predict each next token from the ones before it.
mask/parallel: A transformer can practice on every position at once. Feed in the whole sentence, and ask output i to predict token i plus one.
mask/cheat: But look at the next-word head. Token i can see token i plus one, so it can simply copy the answer, and learn nothing it could use later.
mask/mask: The fix is the causal mask. Before the softmax, add minus infinity to every score where the key comes after the query.
mask/zero: e to the minus infinity is zero, so those keys get no weight at all, and each row still adds up to one.
mask/triangle: The attention matrix becomes a lower triangle. Each token sees itself and its past, and nothing else.
mask/next: With the mask on, the next-word head loses its target, and falls back on the current word.
mask/payoff: Now one pass over a sentence trains every next-token prediction in it at once, with no cheating. An RNN would need one step per token.
mask/generate: When generating, the model writes one token, appends it, and runs again. The mask makes training and generation see the same past.
order/strange: Here is a strange fact. Self-attention has no idea what order its tokens are in.
order/why: The score between cat and mat depends only on their two vectors, not on where they sit.
order/outs: Here is each word's attention output, from our toy example.
order/shuffle: Now shuffle the sentence, and run attention again.
order/moved: Every word gets exactly the same output as before. The rows simply moved along with their words.
order/bag: So the cat sat on the mat, and the mat sat on the cat, look identical to an attention layer. That will not do.
order/fix: The fix: write each token's position into its vector.
positions/add: The original transformer adds a positional encoding to each token: a vector that depends only on its position.
positions/waves: It is built from sine and cosine waves. Each pair of columns gets one wave, and each pair turns at its own speed.
positions/fast: The first pair turns fast, about once every six positions. It tells neighbors apart.
positions/slow: Later pairs turn slower and slower, until the last takes tens of thousands of positions to come around. They tell the start of a document from its middle.
positions/clock: Think of a clock with many hands. Read all the hands together, and every position has its own pattern.
positions/grid: Here are sixty four positions, one per row, across sixty four columns: fast stripes on the left, slow ones on the right.
positions/rotate: Now the clever part. Each sine and cosine pair is a point on a circle, and moving one position forward rotates it by a fixed angle.
positions/linear: A rotation is a matrix multiply. So the code for position p plus k is a fixed linear function of the code for p, the same for every p.
positions/headlink: That is exactly what a W Q can express. Our previous-word head was built that way: its W Q turns every pair back by one step.
positions/bump: It also means the similarity of two positions depends only on how far apart they are, not on where they sit.
positions/today: Later models learned their position vectors instead, and most now rotate the queries and keys directly, a trick called rope, in chapter six.
block/two: Attention moves information between tokens. A block also has to work on each token by itself, and stay trainable when stacked deep.
block/mlp: So after attention comes a small MLP, applied to every token separately, with the same weights.
block/wide: It widens each vector to four times the width, applies a ReLU, and projects back down.
block/residual: Each sublayer sits inside a residual connection: its output is added to its input, instead of replacing it.
block/resnet: That is the trick that made hundred and fifty two layer ResNets trainable. Each sublayer only has to learn a correction, and the gradient has a straight path down.
block/ln: And after each add comes layer norm: shift and scale each token's vector to mean zero and standard deviation one.
block/lnrows: Watch the rows. Whatever comes in, every row leaves with a mean of zero and a spread of one.
block/batch: It is batch norm turned sideways: it normalizes each token over its own features, so it never depends on the batch.
block/shape: A block takes a T by d matrix, and returns one of the same shape. That is what lets blocks stack.
block/stack: The paper stacked six of them. GPT three stacks ninety six.
block/prenorm: One change came later. GPT two moved the layer norm to the start of each sublayer, which trains deep stacks more easily. Chapter six has the details.
families/orig: The original transformer was built for translation, so it has two halves.
families/enc: The encoder reads the source sentence with no mask. Every source token sees every other.
families/dec: The decoder writes the translation, with a causal mask.
families/cross: And each decoder block has a third sublayer, cross-attention. Its queries come from the decoder, its keys and values from the encoder, so every target word can look at the whole source.
families/bert: Later models kept one half. BERT is encoder only: it reads a whole text, and fills in words that were masked out.
families/gpt: GPT is decoder only: one causal stack, trained to predict the next token.
families/today: Today's large language models are almost all decoder only. Predicting the next token turns out to cover translation, summaries and answers too, phrased as text to continue.
params/count: How big is one block? Count its matrices.
params/attn: Attention has four: W Q, W K, W V and W O, each d by d. That is four d squared.
params/mlp: The MLP has two: d by four d, and four d by d. That is eight d squared.
params/twelve: Together, twelve d squared: a third attention, two thirds MLP. Biases and layer norms barely register.
params/gpt2: GPT two small has a width of seven hundred and sixty eight, and twelve blocks. That is about eighty five million in the blocks, plus thirty nine million in the embedding: a hundred and twenty four million in all.
params/gpt3: GPT three has a width of twelve thousand two hundred and eighty eight, and ninety six blocks. That comes to about a hundred and seventy four billion: its famous one seventy five billion.
params/square: Parameters grow with the square of the width, but only in proportion to the depth.
params/compute: And parameters are not the whole cost. The T by T scores have no parameters at all, but their cost grows with the square of the length.
recap/whole: Let us put the whole thing together.
recap/embed: Tokens become vectors, and their positions are added in.
recap/attn: In every block, attention with many heads lets each token gather what it needs from the others, behind a mask if it is a decoder.
recap/scale: Scores are divided by the square root of d k, so the softmax stays soft.
recap/mlp: An MLP works on each token, and residual adds and layer norms keep a deep stack trainable.
recap/out: At the end comes one score per vocabulary word, for the next token.
recap/next: That one block, stacked a few dozen times, is the whole model. Nearly every large language model since twenty eighteen is built from it.
recap/bye: Next, in chapter three: where the token vectors come from.
